title: The Law Committee
hookLine: Conservative rabbis rule on questions like driving to synagogue on Shabbat

lines: SATURDAY, A CAR IN THE DRIVEWAY.
cards: Saturday morning. A family is dressed for synagogue, but the building is across town, too far for the grandmother to walk, too far for the kids. The car sits in the driveway.

For a family that keeps Shabbat, that car is a real question: Shabbat is a day without kindling fire, and rabbis have long treated starting an engine as part of that. Stay home and miss praying with their community?
Or drive, only there and only back? In the Conservative movement, a question like that doesn't get settled at the kitchen table. It goes to a committee.

teach.b: The Law Committee. Its full name is the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, and it belongs to the Conservative movement's association of rabbis. Its job is old work in a new room.
Long before any committee, a Jew with a hard question of law wrote to a scholar, and the scholar wrote back.
The answer is called a teshuvah, a response, and the committee writes teshuvot too: sources, arguments, a conclusion. The text behind the driving question is short.
The Torah says, "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." The hard part was weighing two goods: Shabbat rest, and praying together.
The committee's answer, as it is usually told, was that a family living too far to walk could drive to synagogue on Shabbat, and home again, and nowhere else.
Not because Shabbat matters less, but because losing the community's prayer would cost Shabbat more.

One more thing to know: the committee can approve more than one answer to the same question. Then each congregation's rabbi, called the mara d'atra, the master of the place, chooses which one that community follows.
So some Conservative synagogues accepted the driving ruling, and some Conservative Jews still walk every Shabbat.

teach.h: MORE THAN ONE ANSWER CAN STAND.
teach.b: Orthodox authorities hold that driving on Shabbat is forbidden, and they reach that answer from the same texts.
Two movements, one Torah, different weighings.

how: In the Conservative movement, rabbis bring questions of Jewish law to the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, which answers in written responsa; each congregation's rabbi decides which approved answer the community follows.

games.why: as the ruling is usually told, the committee allowed driving to synagogue and home only. the reason was not that Shabbat matters less, but that losing communal prayer would cost Shabbat more.

practice: Bring back the family and the car, and hold one good in each hand: a day of rest with no engine and no errands, and the grandmother and the kids praying together.
Don't decide; just feel the weight of each, the way a committee has to. Then ask yourself which is harder: judging an answer, or writing one.
